claims.text: Pre-exposure Q235 steel has a naturally formed, relatively thin native iron-oxide surface layer.
The native iron-oxide layer protects Q235 steel and can self-heal minor defects under benign room-temperature conditions.
Aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C destabilizes the native oxide layer on Q235 steel.
At high temperature, aggressive salt acts as a flux that dissolves the protective iron oxide.
Salt exposure transforms the protective iron-oxide phase into less protective compounds.
Flux-assisted dissolution and phase transformation cause oxide spallation.
Salt-induced oxide disruption prevents formation of a continuous, adherent oxide film on Q235 steel.
Loss of a continuous, adherent oxide film accelerates corrosion of Q235 steel.
High-temperature salt-exposed Q235 specimens will have a more degraded and non-uniform oxide layer than specimens exposed at room temperature or at high temperature without salt.
High-temperature salt-exposed Q235 specimens will exhibit greater mass loss than room-temperature specimens and high-temperature specimens exposed without salt.
High-temperature salt-exposed Q235 specimens will exhibit greater surface roughening than room-temperature specimens and high-temperature specimens exposed without salt.
In a high-temperature inert atmosphere without salt, the Q235 oxide layer will remain comparatively intact.
High-temperature inert exposure produces only thermally activated native oxidation, without salt-induced acceleration.
The proposed flux-disruption mechanism should not operate when aggressive salt is absent.
The proposed mechanism should not operate below temperatures sufficient to activate flux-assisted oxide disruption.
Chromium-containing steels may resist this mechanism because chromium enhances oxide stability.
The kinetics and critical threshold of salt-induced degradation can vary with salt chemistry and steel microstructure.

contradictions.description: The reference environment is called inert, yet the baseline assumes thermally activated oxidation occurs there. Without specifying a controlled residual oxygen activity, oxidation in a genuinely inert atmosphere is internally ambiguous.
